title: Evaluating & Deploying Graph-LLM Systems

questions.prompt: In Listing 82.1, what does context precision measure?
options: The share of retrieved items that are relevant
How often the generated answer is correct
How many items the retriever returns per query
The share of ground-truth facts that were retrieved
questions.explanation: Precision divides the overlap by len(retrieved). Recall divides by the number of ground-truth facts.

refLinks.label: §82.2.1 Context Precision and Recall, Adapted for Retrieval Without Generation

questions.prompt: A retriever returns 3 entities. One of them is relevant, and it is the only ground-truth fact. What is the context precision?
questions.explanation: 1 relevant out of 3 retrieved is 0.333. Recall would be 1/1 = 1.0, the single-hop pattern in the results table.

questions.prompt: Why can this chapter score retrieval with no LLM call at all?
options: RAGAS metrics are defined only for retrieval.
Precision and recall need only the question text.
Retrieved entities are checked against ground truth.
The LLM's answers were cached from Chapter 80.
questions.explanation: The definitions match RAGAS, applied to retrieved entities rather than a generated answer. Retrieval can be checked before any generation step exists.

refLinks.label: §82.2.1 Context Precision and Recall, Adapted for Retrieval Without Generation

questions.prompt: The first benchmark version gave GraphRAG 0.0 recall on two single-hop questions. What did that show?
options: GraphRAG can't answer single-hop questions.
Vector-RAG is better on all simple questions.
The graph was missing those two entities.
A bug in the harness, not a GraphRAG weakness
questions.explanation: A property graph answers single-hop questions by direct lookup. With that routing, the two methods tied.

refLinks.label: §82.2.2 A Fair Comparison Requires Giving Each Method Its Right Tool

questions.prompt: What is the common mistake Procedure 82.2 warns against?
options: Scoring both methods with the same metrics
Routing questions by shape before scoring them
Including single-hop questions in a GraphRAG benchmark
Reporting a wrong-tool score as a method finding
questions.explanation: That low score is a harness bug, not a result. Like testing a calculator on essay questions.

refLinks.label: §82.2.2 A Fair Comparison Requires Giving Each Method Its Right Tool

questions.prompt: One multi-hop question had a vendor purchasing directly from the flagged entity. How was it fixed?
options: The scoring function was changed to accept the one-hop answer.
A third vendor was added so the pattern existed.
The question was relabelled as unanswerable.
The question was dropped from the benchmark.
questions.explanation: Forcing a wrong answer through scoring would hide the problem. The graph was fixed so the question tested what it claimed.

refLinks.label: §82.2.3 A Second Bug the Benchmark Itself Had

questions.prompt: Which checks does Procedure 82.3 ask for on each benchmark question? Select all that apply.
options: Is the question longer than a set number of words?
Does the question favour GraphRAG over vector-RAG?
Does the intended answer pattern exist in the graph as built?
Before blaming the system for "no valid answer", is the ground truth right?
Is the hop shape what the question text implies?
questions.explanation: Ground truth gets the same scrutiny as the system. Which method a question favours and its length aren't checks in the procedure.

questions.prompt: How does each method's cost per query behave, per §82.2.4?
options: Both grow with the number of hops.
Vector-RAG is fixed. GraphRAG varies.
GraphRAG is constant, while vector-RAG grows with the question length.
Both are constant per query.
questions.explanation: Vector-RAG scored all 16 passages every time. GraphRAG averaged 3.8 operations, which depends on fan-out near the anchor.

refLinks.label: §82.2.4 Cost Isn’t Free to Ignore, Even When It Favours GraphRAG Here

questions.prompt: GraphRAG was cheaper on the 9-node graph. What does the chapter conclude from that?
options: GraphRAG is always cheaper than vector-RAG.
Cost doesn't matter once precision is higher.
Vector-RAG should be avoided on small graphs.
Nothing general. Big graphs could invert it.
questions.explanation: It is a property of this graph's size. Cost has to be measured on the graph actually deployed.

refLinks.label: §82.2.4 Cost Isn’t Free to Ignore, Even When It Favours GraphRAG Here

questions.prompt: Traversal took 0.027 ms at 100 nodes and 2.346 ms at 100,000 nodes. Roughly how many times slower is the larger graph, from these two numbers?
questions.explanation: 2.346 / 0.027 is about 86.9, close to the reported 87.5x from unrounded timings. A 1,000x larger graph cost under 100x more time.

questions.prompt: Which are the chapter's reasons to move from networkx to a managed graph database? Select all that apply.
options: Durability and backup guarantees
Access control
Concurrent query load from many users
A graph too large for one process's memory
Traversal speed at 100,000 nodes
questions.explanation: Traversal stayed under 2.5 ms at 100,000 nodes, so speed alone isn't the reason. A single-process timing loop can't test the others.

refLinks.label: §82.2.5 The Scaling Benchmark Answers a Different Question Than “Is It Fast?”

questions.prompt: What did the benchmark show on single-hop questions?
options: An exact tie on precision and recall
Vector-RAG well ahead on precision
Both methods scored zero recall
GraphRAG well ahead on precision and recall
questions.explanation: Once each method had its right tool, GraphRAG cost nothing on the questions vector-RAG already handles.

questions.prompt: What is the right claim to generalise from the benchmark?
options: Vector-RAG is better for production systems.
The two methods perform the same overall.
GraphRAG is better than vector-RAG.
GraphRAG wins on relationship questions.
questions.explanation: Parity on single-hop, a large gap on multi-hop (0.778 vs 0.167 precision). The advantage is concentrated, not blanket.

bookExercises.prompt: State the RAGAS-style definitions of context precision and context recall, and explain why they can be computed here without any generation step.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Context recall: the fraction of ground-truth facts present in the retrieved context. Context precision: the fraction of retrieved chunks/entities that are relevant. Both can be computed here without any generation step because they're defined purely in terms of what was retrieved versus what should have been retrieved. No downstream generated answer is needed to compute either metric, only the retrieval output and a ground-truth reference.

bookExercises.prompt: State the measured single-hop and multi-hop precision/recall numbers for vector-RAG vs. GraphRAG from the Worked Example, and summarise the pattern in one sentence.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Single-hop: vector-RAG 0.333/1.000, GraphRAG 0.333/1.000 (exact tie). Multi-hop: vector-RAG 0.167/0.312, GraphRAG 0.778/1.000 (GraphRAG far ahead). Pattern: GraphRAG matches vector-RAG exactly where vector-RAG already works (single-hop) and wins by roughly an order of magnitude on precision where it doesn't (multi-hop).

bookExercises.prompt: Using the Worked Example's harness-bug finding (GraphRAG scoring 0.0 recall on single-hop questions before the fix), explain why this result was correctly diagnosed as an evaluation-harness bug rather than a genuine finding about GraphRAG's capability.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: The 0.0 recall on single-hop questions was diagnosed as a harness bug, not a genuine finding, because GraphRAG was being scored using ONLY the multi-hop pattern-matching function (a tool never designed to answer single-hop questions) rather than being given the appropriate direct entity-lookup tool a real graph-RAG system would actually use for that question shape. The failure reflected a mismatch between the question and the tool applied to it, not any real limitation of graph-based retrieval on single-hop questions, exactly analogous to testing a calculator on essay questions and reporting that it "failed."

bookExercises.prompt: Using the Worked Example's operations-per-query result (vector-RAG 16.0 constant, GraphRAG 3.8 average), explain specifically why this cost comparison should NOT be generalised to a production knowledge graph with millions of nodes, connecting your answer to what "average" and "constant" mean for each method's scaling behaviour.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Vector-RAG's cost is constant (16 operations) because it always scores every passage against the query regardless of graph/dataset structure. This scales with the total number of passages, not with any particular question's complexity. GraphRAG's cost (3.8 average) varies with the local graph structure near the anchor entity, specifically, how many neighbours/hops need to be examined to answer a given question. On a production graph with millions of nodes, a highly-connected anchor entity (e.g., a large corporation with thousands of subsidiaries or vendors) could require examining a traversal fan-out far larger than 16, while vector-RAG's constant-per-query cost wouldn't change with graph size at all. The comparison measured here could straightforwardly invert at larger, differently-shaped graphs, which is exactly why "GraphRAG is cheaper" can't be generalized past the specific 9-node graph it was measured on.

bookExercises.prompt: A team reads this chapter's traversal-speed benchmark (87.5x slowdown for 1000x more nodes, still under 2.5ms) and concludes "we don't need a managed graph database, self-hosted networkx scales fine." Using this chapter's Trade-offs section, write the two or three sentences you'd say about what that conclusion misses.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: "This chapter's own benchmark explicitly says the traversal-speed measurement doesn't test the actual reasons production systems migrate to a managed graph database: concurrent query load from many simultaneous users, a graph too large to fit in one process's memory, durability/backup guarantees, and access control, none of which a single-process timing loop can show. 'Fast enough for one process, one query at a time' and 'ready for production' are different claims, and this benchmark only answers the first one."

bookExercises.prompt: Procedure 82.3 warns that a "no valid answer" benchmark result can mean either a system failure or a benchmark ground-truth error. Using this chapter's Solaris Energy question example, describe what evidence should be checked to distinguish between these two explanations before reporting a result.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: To distinguish a system failure from a benchmark ground-truth error for the Solaris Energy question, check whether the intended answer pattern actually exists in the graph as constructed. Trace the specific entities and relationships the question implies should connect, and verify that path is genuinely present. In this chapter's case, that check revealed the graph had Solaris Energy purchasing directly from the flagged vendor (a one-hop fact), not from a sibling vendor sharing a parent with the flagged one (the intended two-hop fact), meaning no valid two-hop answer existed for the question as worded, which is a benchmark construction error, not a retrieval system failure, and the fix was adding a genuine third vendor to the graph so the intended pattern actually existed.

bookExercises.prompt: Read about RAGAS's original context precision/recall definitions (Es et al., 2023) as applied to a full generation pipeline, not just retrieval. Explain in your own words what additional failure mode a full RAGAS evaluation (including faithfulness and answer relevance) could catch that this chapter's retrieval-only evaluation cannot.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: A full RAGAS evaluation adds faithfulness (is every claim in the generated answer supported by the retrieved context?) and answer relevance (does the generated answer actually address the question asked?) on top of retrieval-only precision/recall. This chapter's retrieval-only evaluation can confirm the right facts were retrieved, but it cannot catch a generation-stage failure where the LLM ignores good retrieved context and hallucinates an unsupported answer anyway, or where the LLM produces a technically-faithful-but-off-topic response that doesn't actually address what was asked. Both failure modes require actually running the generation step and checking its output against the retrieved context, which a purely retrieval-focused evaluation like this chapter's structurally cannot surface.
